questions.prompt: A laboratory measures receptive fields in two visual areas and finds that fields in the second area are, on average, four times larger than in the first, with no anatomical tracer work. A reviewer concludes that the two areas form a two-stage hierarchy. What is the strongest objection to that conclusion?
questions.answer: Pooling alone enlarges receptive fields, so the size difference could arise from a common input source or from parallel streams rather than from the second area receiving convergent projections from the first.
questions.distractor: The objection fails because receptive field size is determined by the number of neurons in an area, and a larger area necessarily sits above a smaller one.
questions.correction: Receptive field size is a property of what a unit pools, and any arrangement that pools inputs produces larger fields, including a parallel arrangement in which both areas draw from a common earlier stage. A hierarchy claim is a directed-convergence claim, so it needs projection evidence, which is exactly what the study lacks. The distractor substitutes a counting claim for an ordering claim: neuron number and territory size answer a magnification question, not a question about which area projects to which.

questions.prompt: An engineer designs an auditory prosthesis that estimates source direction by measuring the arrival time of sound at two microphones spaced 0.18 metres apart, and is puzzled that the estimate becomes erratic for high-frequency sounds. Using the physics in the lesson, explain the cause and the design change indicated.
questions.answer: At high frequencies the sound's period becomes shorter than the maximum arrival difference of roughly half a millisecond, so the timing measurement becomes cycle-ambiguous; the indicated change is to use the level difference between the two microphones for high frequencies.
questions.distractor: The microphones are too close together to register any arrival difference at high frequencies, so the spacing should be increased until the delay exceeds one period at the target frequency.
questions.correction: Spacing of 0.18 metres already produces a delay of about half a millisecond, which is a large fraction of a period at low frequencies; the problem is ambiguity, not absence. Increasing the spacing widens the maximum delay, which makes the ambiguity worse rather than better, because the delay then spans even more cycles. The correct reading of the physics is that a fixed delay must be compared with a period that shrinks as frequency rises, which is why biological systems use timing at low frequencies and level differences at high ones.

questions.prompt: A researcher records from a single rapidly adapting mechanoreceptor and finds that it fires twice, at the onset and the offset of a held indentation. She concludes that this afferent is the brain's signal for the duration of contact. Which further result is required before the word signal is doing any work?
questions.answer: Evidence about readout, showing that the percept of contact duration follows this afferent's activity when the rest of the population responding to the same contact is held constant or manipulated.
questions.distractor: A larger sample of the same afferent class, since repeating the recording in more units would establish that the afferent class carries the duration signal.
questions.correction: Repeating the observation establishes that the response profile is typical of the class, which is a fact about the receptor rather than about the brain's use of it. Because receptive fields overlap and many afferents respond to the same contact, a population readout is fully compatible with every unit also having a characteristic temporal profile. The distinction that matters is between a fibre's response profile, an anatomical channel arrangement, and a perceptual readout, and only the third is a claim about what the brain knows.

questions.prompt: Two people receive identical stimuli to identical skin sites in a controlled experiment and report pain that differs by more than a factor of two. One researcher says the difference must be measurement noise. Using the double pain and modulation evidence, evaluate that response.
questions.answer: It is not sufficient as an explanation, because the same peripheral input can produce different transmission depending on converging afferent and descending inputs, so a large between-person difference is an expected property of the system that requires a design that varies modulation rather than an appeal to noise.
questions.distractor: It is sufficient, because identical stimuli must produce identical nociceptor activity and therefore identical pain, so any difference is error.
questions.correction: The premise is half right: identical stimuli do produce comparable nociceptor activation, and the error is the step from that to identical pain. Two channels with different conduction speeds produce two distinct sensations from one stimulus, which already shows that input and experience are not in one-to-one correspondence, and descending and converging inputs modulate how much of the nociceptive signal is transmitted. A factor-of-two difference therefore needs an explanation in terms of modulation or central processing, and a design that manipulates or measures modulation is what would test such an account. Note also that appeals to noise are testable and should be supported by an estimate of variability, not asserted.

questions.prompt: A device reports head orientation by integrating the signal from a sensor that measures angular acceleration and whose output decays with a five-second time constant. After about fifteen seconds of steady rotation the reported orientation has drifted far from the true value. What does this demonstrate about the sense the device is imitating?
questions.answer: That an acceleration signal must be combined with other evidence, such as gravity-referenced or visual signals, because integration of a decaying signal cannot sustain a position estimate during prolonged motion.
questions.distractor: That the sensor is faulty, since a correctly functioning position sensor would not produce drift over fifteen seconds of steady motion.
questions.correction: No physical sensor of this kind reports position; the canals report angular acceleration through fluid displacement and cupula deflection, and the time constant is a property of the mechanics rather than a defect. Three time constants of about five seconds each give a decay to about 5 per cent of the initial response, which is the arithmetic behind the drift. The lesson's point is that the biological system faces the same problem and solves it by combining several partial signals, which is why the sense of position is an integration rather than a readout and why its characteristic errors appear in rotating-chair experiments.

units.title: Inside the body and outside the moment: regulation, timing, and a contested metaphor

lessons.title: Movement is planned before it is executed
lessons.explanation: Objective: describe the evidence that movement is prepared in advance, identify the structures that carry preparation, explain what a forward model is for, and say precisely what the timing experiments on voluntary action do and do not establish. Start with a structural fact from Neuroscience Online, Section 3, Chapter 3: section 3.2 states that motor cortex comprises the primary motor cortex, the premotor cortex and the supplementary motor area, and figure 3.1 shows these areas in lateral, dorsal and medial views. Section 3.5 'Encoding of Movement by Motor Cortex' covers directional tuning and the velocity profile of targeted movements in figures 3.8 and 3.9, and figure 3.10 is captioned as showing premotor cortex neurons signalling preparation for movement. That figure is the anatomical and physiological core of the lesson: cells in premotor areas carry activity that depends on what the animal is about to do rather than on what it is doing now. Chapter 5 provides the control-theory vocabulary. Section 5.6 'Cerebellum and Control Systems' asks what the symptoms of cerebellar damage tell us about the computation, figure 5.9 draws a feedback control system such as a home thermostat, and figure 5.10 states that a feedforward control system is needed for fast movements because feedback arrives too late. That single sentence contains the whole argument for prediction: conduction delays mean that a controller which waited for sensory feedback would initiate every correction after the body had already moved, so the system must act on a prediction of the consequences of its own command.
lessons.example: Compute the delay that makes prediction necessary, then examine the timing experiment that makes prediction controversial. A correction loop has to carry a signal out to the muscle and back from the sensors. Take a distance of about one metre from the spinal cord to a hand and back, and note that the fastest human afferents conduct at roughly 60 to 70 metres per second in the largest fibres while motor axons conduct somewhat more slowly, so use an illustrative round-trip speed of about 60 metres per second. The round-trip time is then about 2 divided by 60 seconds, which is about 0.033 seconds, or 33 milliseconds, before any central processing time is added. A deliberate voluntary reaction to an unpredictable stimulus, as measured in simple reaction-time tasks, is commonly of the order of 200 milliseconds, which is roughly six times the conduction delay, so most of the delay is central rather than peripheral. Meanwhile a fast reach takes on the order of 300 to 500 milliseconds. A controller with a 33-to-200-millisecond loop and a 400-millisecond movement has time for only a few corrections, so most of the trajectory must be computed in advance, and that is what feedforward control means. Now the controversy. In the classic experiments, a readiness potential begins over the scalp hundreds of milliseconds before a self-initiated movement, and participants report the moment they became aware of the intention at around 200 milliseconds before the movement. Subtracting, the gap between the onset of the potential and the reported intention is of the order of 350 milliseconds. That subtraction is what the strong claim that the brain decides before you do rests on. Read the source note on the 2012 accumulator model in the readings before accepting it, because that paper shows how the average readiness potential could arise from ongoing noise crossing a decision threshold rather than from a specific command.
lessons.question: A commentator writes that readiness potential experiments show that conscious decisions to move occur after the brain has already decided, so free will is an illusion. Which single feature of the experiments most undermines that inference as stated?
lessons.answer: The reported time of awareness is itself an estimate taken from the participant's own report of a rapidly moving clock, and the readiness potential is an averaged slow signal over many trials whose onset can be produced by the random accumulation of neural noise toward a decision threshold rather than by a specific decision signal.
lessons.distractor: The experiments are invalid because the readiness potential is only about 10 microvolts and a signal that small cannot carry any information.
lessons.correction: Amplitude is not the issue; the signal is small but averaged over many trials it is reliable, and small signals carry information elsewhere in neuroscience. The inference fails for two more specific reasons. First, the dependent measure is a subjective report of a clock position, and reports of events only a few hundred milliseconds apart are noisy and can be systematically shifted by attention, so the gap being interpreted is itself uncertain. Second, averaging across trials produces a slow ramp whether or not each individual trial contains a discrete decision event, so an onset in the average does not license the claim that a decision occurred at that moment in each trial. Both points are about the inference from measurement to conclusion, which is exactly what a claim about agency requires.

depth.definitions: Motor planning is activity in advance of a movement that specifies some part of the upcoming action. The primary motor cortex is the main cortical source of the corticospinal projection; the premotor cortex and the supplementary motor area lie adjacent and are associated with preparing and sequencing movements. A forward model is an internal process that predicts the sensory consequences of a motor command before they occur; an inverse model or controller is a process that computes the command needed to reach a desired state. Feedback control uses measured error from the actual movement to correct it; feedthrough or feedforward control uses a prediction instead. The readiness potential is a slow scalp potential recorded in the second or so before a self-initiated movement. The sense of agency is the experience of having caused one's own action. Prerequisites: the reflex loop and feedback regulation (lesson 38), and the general warning about interpreting averaged signals (lesson 27).
depth.mechanism: The mechanistic case for planning rests on three converging lines. Anatomically, premotor and supplementary motor areas project to primary motor cortex and to the spinal cord and contain cells whose activity ramps up before an instructed movement, as figure 3.10 illustrates. Physiologically, the delays computed above make purely feedback control inadequate for fast movements, which is exactly the argument in figure 5.10, so some prediction is required. Computationally, the cerebellum has long been proposed as the site of a forward model: it receives a copy of the motor command and information about the resulting state and can compare the two, which is how a predictor can be trained. The 2021 review in Frontiers in Systems Neuroscience by Welniarz, Worbe and Gallea develops this proposal and also links it to the sense of agency, and it should be read as a unifying theoretical proposal rather than a measured result, because the review's own framing is that the theory links several phenomena. The strongest limitation to state is that the readiness potential literature is genuinely contested. The 2012 PNAS paper by Schurger, Sitt and Dehaene, in this lesson's readings, proposes that the pre-movement ramp can emerge because ongoing stochastic neural activity is accumulated to a threshold, so the average ramp does not require a specific decision signal that precedes awareness. That proposal does not settle the metaphysical question, and it does show that the inference from the averaged waveform to the claim about agency is not forced.
depth.secondExample: Take a contrasting case where prediction is directly visible in behaviour: catching a ball. The ball is moving fast, so by the time a visual signal reaches the cortex and a correction reaches the arm, the ball has moved further, and a person who reacted only to the current position would arrive late and low. Predictable interception therefore requires extrapolating the trajectory, comparing it with the planned reach, and adjusting before the error appears. Compare that with a slow, self-paced movement such as reaching for a mug on a table. Here feedback is affordable, the movement can be corrected continuously, and a person who could not predict at all would still manage, only less smoothly. The contrast is the diagnostic tool of the lesson: it tells you when to expect planning to be visible, which is when the movement is fast, novel or unpredictable, and when to expect sensory feedback to dominate, which is when the environment is stable and time is plentiful. The cerebellar figures for feedback and feedforward control map directly onto the two cases, and the suggested reading on self-motion restoration in lesson 55 shows the same logic in the vestibular reflex, where a prediction-driven compensation keeps the image stable during natural movement.
depth.mistake: The common error is a false dichotomy: either movements are fully planned in advance and feedback is decoration, or movements are feedback-driven and the notion of a plan is an artifact of averaging. Diagnose it by asking what the system should do when the environment changes unexpectedly during a movement, for example when a held object turns out to be heavier than predicted. A fully planned controller would complete the original trajectory regardless, and a purely feedback controller would have no basis for the initial command. What actually happens is that the initial command is issued from a prediction and then revised when the mismatch signal arrives, which is a hybrid. The correction is to treat planning and feedback as components with different time constants rather than as competing explanations. A second common error is to read the readiness potential timing as establishing that the brain decided, which the accumulator model shows is an additional assumption.
depth.application: Nonblocking task, done at a desk, with no heavy or sharp objects. Write a one-page prediction audit of an everyday action of your choice, for example catching a thrown object or typing a familiar sentence. Address four points. First, decompose the action into a planned component and a feedback component, and state for each the time available and the delay of the loop involved, using the 33-millisecond conduction estimate from the lesson and stating that it is illustrative. Second, name the specific signals that a forward model would have to predict for this action, and name the signal that would reveal a prediction error. Third, describe what a person with impaired prediction would do differently, in terms of the observable behaviour rather than the anatomy. Fourth, state one measurement that would distinguish a hybrid account from a purely feedback account, and one that would distinguish it from a purely planned account. Self-review rubric: full credit requires a delay comparison with the arithmetic shown, at least two named predicted signals, a purely-observable description of impaired prediction, and two discriminating measurements. No credit for a page that concludes that movement is 'mostly automatic'.
depth.summary: Movement is prepared in advance because the wiring makes feedback too slow to control fast actions, and premotor and supplementary motor areas carry activity that depends on the upcoming movement rather than on its execution. Feedforward prediction, most likely involving the cerebellum, supplies the estimate of consequences that the loop cannot deliver in time, and the sense of agency is plausibly related to comparing that prediction with the outcome. The contested part is the interpretation of the readiness potential timing: an averaged slow ramp before a self-initiated movement does not by itself show that a decision preceded awareness, because accumulating noisy activity to a threshold produces the same average. The transferable skill is to separate a measured timing interval from the claim about causation that a commentator wants to build on it.

lessons.title: Interoception and the immune-to-brain conversation
lessons.explanation: Objective: explain how the brain receives information about the internal state of the body, describe the routes by which immune signals reach the brain despite the blood-brain barrier, and evaluate the claim that individuals differ in how accurately they perceive internal signals, noting that the measurement of that difference is contested. Interoception means sensing the state of the body's interior, including signals arising from the cardiovascular, respiratory, gastrointestinal and other systems. The anatomy constrains the story. Neuroscience Online, Section 4, Chapter 11, section 11.1 'Blood-brain Barrier Maintains the Constancy of the Brain's Internal Environment' explains that the barrier restricts the passage of many circulating molecules, which immediately raises a problem for any account in which blood-borne signals inform the brain directly. Section 11.4 'Circumventricular Organs' supplies part of the answer: in a few specialised regions the barrier is absent or different, so circulating substances can act on neurons there, and the area postrema is the classical example of a site where blood-borne signals are detected and where a signalling pathway to vomiting is initiated. A second route is neural, since peripheral nerves including the vagus carry information from the viscera. A third is local signalling at the barrier itself, in which cells associated with the vessel wall respond to circulating molecules and pass a signal inward. The immune system uses all three. The 2026 review by Lee, Ko and Um in Experimental and Molecular Medicine, 'Cytokine-mediated immune-to-brain signaling in neural circuit disorders', describes how systemic inflammation changes cytokine signalling that reaches neural circuits and how microglial states shift in response. Read it as a recent review of an active field rather than as a settled pathway diagram.
lessons.example: Work the measurement problem, because it is where a plausible idea becomes a contested construct. Interoceptive accuracy is usually estimated by comparing a measure of internal signal against a report. A common method is heartbeat counting: the participant counts heartbeats over a fixed interval without feeling the pulse, and the count is compared with the electrocardiogram. Suppose a participant counts 48 beats in 60 seconds while the recorded heart rate is 60 beats per minute. The ratio is 48 divided by 60, which is 0.8, often reported as 80 per cent accuracy. Now examine what that number depends on. It depends on the participant's belief about their own heart rate, because someone who assumes a rate of about 70 per minute will produce a count near 70 regardless of their actual interoceptive signal. It also depends on the scoring rule, since different published rules transform the same pair of numbers into different scores, and on the interval chosen. The 2019 article by Murphy, Catmur and Bird in Psychonomic Bulletin and Review on classifying individual differences in interoception addresses exactly this: it argues that measures of interoception need to be separated into distinct components, so that what a task indexes is not assumed to be a single capacity. Two arithmetic consequences follow. First, because a score is an interval ratio, it will drift with the assumed heart rate even if the underlying signal is unchanged. Second, because the score is a ratio of two small numbers, its reliability is limited, and a single session cannot support a strong claim about a stable trait. Both points are computed from the structure of the measure, not from a specific dataset.
lessons.question: A study finds that participants with higher heartbeat-counting accuracy also report stronger emotional intensity, and concludes that interoceptive accuracy causes emotional intensity. Which feature of the design most limits that conclusion, and what would the correction be?
lessons.answer: Heartbeat counting can be performed using beliefs about heart rate rather than an internal signal, so a correlation with the tendency to attend to and report on the body may reflect that reporting style; the correction is to use a task that controls for knowledge of heart rate and to separate the components of interoception that the measure is claimed to index.
lessons.distractor: The correlation is too small to matter, because only correlations above about 0.9 are meaningful in psychology.
lessons.correction: Effect size is not the issue, and there is no threshold above which a correlation becomes causal. The specific problem is that the task can be solved without the capacity it is supposed to measure, so the correlate may be the strategy or the self-report tendency rather than the underlying sensitivity. Adding a condition that manipulates or measures the participant's belief about their heart rate, and treating the measure's components separately as Murphy and colleagues argue, is the correction. Note the wider point: a correlation between two measured quantities cannot establish direction, so a causal claim needs an intervention or a design that varies one while holding the other fixed.

depth.definitions: Interoception is the sensing of internal bodily state. Interoceptive accuracy is performance on a task that requires detecting an internal signal; interoceptive sensibility is the person's belief about their own interoceptive ability, typically measured by questionnaire; interoceptive awareness is sometimes used for the correspondence between the two, though usage across the literature is inconsistent. The blood-brain barrier is the set of properties of brain vasculature that restricts the passage of circulating molecules. Circumventricular organs are specialised midline structures where the barrier is modified, allowing circulating signals to act on neurons. Cytokines are small signalling proteins released by immune and other cells; systemic inflammation means inflammation in the body outside the central nervous system. Sickness behaviour is the coordinated set of changes in activity, appetite, social interest and sleep that often accompanies illness and that can be produced by immune signalling. Prerequisites: the barrier and cerebral metabolism as an environment (lesson 40's method caution and this lesson's reading), and feedback regulation of a physiological variable (lesson 38).
depth.mechanism: Four routes carry internal information centrally and they differ in speed and specificity. Humoral routes use substances that either cross at circumventricular organs or act on barrier-associated cells, which is why the area postrema can detect a circulating toxin and initiate emesis. Neural routes use the vagus and other peripheral nerves, which transmit information about visceral state within milliseconds and provide a labelled channel rather than a diffuse one. Immune routes use cytokines, whose central effects include the coordinated behavioural changes seen in illness, and the review in this lesson's readings describes how systemic inflammation reprograms signalling to neural circuits. Sensory routes include the receptors of the position and pain systems. Stated as a limit: the existence of each route is well-evidenced, while the rules by which the brain weights and combines them into a felt state, and how much of a given percept depends on each, remain active research questions. Read the review for its account of microglial state transitions and synaptic effects, and notice how strongly its conclusions depend on animal models and on the specific molecules investigated, which is a general caution in immune-to-brain work rather than a defect of that one paper.
depth.secondExample: Take a contrasting case where an internal signal is made available to the participant in an unambiguous way and see how the inference changes: the perception of breathlessness under a resistive load. Here the relevant variable, the effort of breathing, is experimentally imposed and measurable, so a claim that participants can detect a change does not depend on their beliefs about their own physiology. Compare the design with heartbeat counting. In the loaded-breathing design the experimenter controls the independent variable and the participant reports a percept, so the relation between stimulus and report is observable; in heartbeat counting the participant both generates and reports the signal, which is precisely why belief contaminates the measure. A second contrast is the cold-pressor or interoceptive-precision literature, where again a stimulus is delivered and the report compared with it. Use this contrast whenever you read a claim about individual differences in interoception: ask whether the internal signal was independently measured, and if it was not, treat the accuracy score as a combination of signal and belief rather than as a clean index.
depth.mistake: The most widespread error is to read 'interoceptive accuracy' as a single stable trait of a person, on the model of a sense organ's sensitivity, and then to interpret a low score as insensitivity to the body. Diagnose it by asking what the score would be for a participant who has strong internal signals but believes their heart rate is 70 and counts accordingly: the score would be driven by the belief, not the signal, so a low or high score does not map onto sensitivity as the trait interpretation requires. A related error is the deterministic cytokine story, in which one molecule is said to cause one feeling, for example inflammation causing low mood. The evidence supports cytokine involvement in coordinated sickness behaviour, and it does not support a single-molecule account of any particular mood, because the effects are dose-, time- and context-dependent and many other systems are involved. The correction in both cases is to keep the measurement, the construct and the mechanism separate, and to state which one a given study actually addressed.
depth.application: Nonblocking task, and this is an educational literature exercise rather than a protocol for interpreting your own symptoms, which belongs with a clinician. Find one published study that reports a correlation between a measure of interoceptive accuracy and an emotional or clinical outcome. Write one page addressing four points. First, state precisely how the internal signal was measured and whether the participant could have used knowledge or belief instead of sensing. Second, list the score transform that was applied and state whether the reported result would survive a different published transform, giving your reasoning from the numbers in the study rather than from its conclusion. Third, name one plausible third variable that could produce the correlation. Fourth, propose a design change that would address the third variable. Self-review rubric: full credit requires an explicit statement about whether the internal signal was independently measured, a reasoned rather than asserted statement about the scoring transform, and a third variable that is genuinely confounded rather than merely mentioned. No credit for a page that treats the accuracy score as a validated measure of a personal trait.
depth.summary: The brain learns about the body's interior through several channels that differ in speed and specificity: barrier-associated and circumventricular detection of circulating molecules, neural routes through the vagus and other nerves, local signalling at the vessel wall, and the sensory systems. Immune signals use the same routes, which is why systemic inflammation can produce coordinated changes in behaviour, and the cytokine literature is active and model-dependent rather than settled. Interoceptive accuracy is a plausible construct whose measurement is genuinely contested, because tasks can be solved using beliefs about the body, and different scoring rules produce different numbers from the same data. The transferable discipline is to ask of any interoception claim whether the internal signal was independently measured, and to keep the measure, the construct and the mechanism apart.

lessons.title: How the brain regulates temperature, hunger and thirst
lessons.explanation: Objective: describe the logic of physiological regulation for three variables, state what a set point claim means and why weight regulation is not best described that way, and explain why a regulated variable can be held steady without any controller aiming at a fixed value. Begin with temperature, where the regulatory architecture is clearest. Neuroscience Online, Section 4, Chapter 3, section 3.4 'Neuronal Mechanism for Body Temperature Set-Point' describes the master circuit, and 3.5 'Mechanism of Change for Body Temperature Set-Point During Fever' is the section that repays careful reading, because it makes the crucial move: in fever the regulated level is changed rather than the regulation being broken. Section 3.8 on disorders of thermoregulation and section 3.7 on emergencies such as hypothermia give the failure modes. Temperature is a good starting case because the variable is a single number that is continuously measurable, the effectors are identifiable, and the loop is closed, so the reasoning can be checked at each step. Feeding is the second case, and there the architecture is contested. Section 4.1 'Theories of Caloric Homeostasis' presents two hypotheses for how caloric balance is achieved, and 4.2 'Mechanisms of Satiety' describes the hypothalamic circuitry and the signals that terminate a meal, while section 4.5 summarises the chapter's position that caloric homeostasis is maintained by a body weight set point. That position is exactly the claim that a 2010 review in this lesson's readings disputes, so the honest instruction is to read the textbook account as one framing and then read the argument against it. The third case, thirst, has the same structure as temperature, with a regulated variable, receptors that detect deviations, and effectors that restore it.
lessons.example: Compute the energetics of a fever and then the arithmetic of a claimed weight change, because the contrast between the two cases is the lesson. For the fever: suppose a person of 70 kilograms has a core temperature raised by 1.5 degrees Celsius, from 36.8 to 38.3. The specific heat of the human body is commonly given as roughly 3470 joules per kilogram per degree Celsius. The energy required to warm the body by that amount is 70 multiplied by 3470 multiplied by 1.5, which is about 364,000 joules, or about 364 kilojoules. Converting to food calories by dividing by 4184 joules per kilocalorie gives about 87 kilocalories. That is the arithmetic reason a fever raises metabolic demand and why shivering is an efficient way to generate heat quickly: the body must raise the temperature of its whole mass, and the cost scales with mass and with the size of the shift. Now the weight claim. A common rule of thumb asserts that about 3500 kilocalories of energy surplus corresponds to one pound of body mass. At a surplus of 500 kilocalories per day, the prediction is 500 divided by 3500, which is 0.143 pounds per day, and multiplied by 365 that is about 52 pounds per year. The arithmetic is unarguable and the premise is wrong as a long-run prediction, because as mass changes the energy cost of moving that mass changes too, so the surplus itself falls; a linear extrapolation of this kind is exactly the mistake the review in the readings addresses. The contrast is the lesson: the fever computation rests on a variable held within a narrow range by a closed loop with known effectors, while the weight rule treats a regulated system as if it were an open one.
lessons.question: A textbook states that body weight is defended at a set point of about 70 kilograms and that deviation produces corrective changes in intake. A reviewer replies that the evidence supports settling points rather than a set point. What is the substantive difference between the two claims, and what observation would distinguish them?
lessons.answer: A set point claims that a specific target value is represented and defended, whereas a settling point claims that weight settles where intake and expenditure balance and shifts when the environment or physiology changes the balance; the distinguishing observation is whether the system returns to the same value after the environment that produced the weight is removed.
lessons.distractor: There is no substantive difference, because both terms describe a stable weight and stability is the only property that matters.
lessons.correction: Stability is common to both accounts and is therefore not the discriminator. The set point account makes the additional claim that a target is encoded and that deviations drive corrective action proportional to the deviation, which predicts a return to the original value. The settling point account predicts only that the system comes to rest where the flows balance, so removing an environmental influence that had raised intake should let weight settle at a lower value without any restoration of an encoded target. A further distinction is that a true set point should defend the value against a wide range of perturbations, whereas a settling point predicts that sustained changes in the environment produce sustained changes in the resting value. The review in this lesson's readings argues that the evidence in humans fits a picture with feedback and settling components rather than a single defended value.

depth.definitions: Physiological regulation is the adjustment of effectors to keep a variable in a workable range. A set point is a claimed target value that a controller defends, with error computed as the deviation from it. A settling point is the value at which inflows and outflows balance, with no encoded target required. Negative feedback is a loop in which a deviation produces a response that reduces the deviation. Anticipatory or feedforward regulation changes behaviour before the deviation occurs, for example drinking before dehydration is measurable. Homeostasis is the maintenance of internal variables within ranges compatible with function; allostasis is a related framing emphasising prediction and adjustment of the defended level according to circumstances. Satiety signals terminate a meal; adiposity signals reflect longer-term energy stores. Prerequisites: reflex loops, feedback and the limits of the set point framing (lesson 38), and the earlier treatment of stress physiology as dose- and context-dependent (lesson 44).
depth.mechanism: For temperature, the mechanism has four identifiable parts: sensors in the skin and in the central nervous system that respond to temperature, a central integration site in the hypothalamus's preoptic region, effectors including shivering, skin blood flow and sweating, and a comparison between the sensed temperature and the regulated level. The chapter's account of fever shows that the comparison is against an adjustable level, which is why a person with a rising fever feels cold and shivers even while their temperature is climbing: the deviation is between their current temperature and a level that has just been raised. For feeding, the signals are more heterogeneous. Short-term signals from the gut and from circulating nutrients influence meal size, and longer-term signals related to fat stores influence intake over weeks. The hypothalamic circuits in section 4.2 integrate these. The contested part is the target. The 2010 review by Müller, Bosy-Westphal and Heymsfield in F1000 Medicine Reports examines whether human body weight is regulated to a set point and concludes that the evidence fits a combination, which is why its own section heading proposes 'set point and settling points' rather than one or the other. State the limitation: the mechanisms are well-characterised at the level of individual signals and circuits, and the level at which the system as a whole is controlled remains an inference, which is why a disagreement about set points is a disagreement about interpretation of the same physiology rather than about the data.
depth.secondExample: Take thirst, which sits between the two cases in tractability and shows what antiregulation means. A person who has lost fluid or eaten salt will drink before the deficit is measurable in blood concentration in some circumstances, which is anticipatory regulation, and the drinking stops before the deficit is fully corrected, which shows the controller is tracking multiple signals rather than one. Now take the hunger-and-thirst contrast that a 2022 PNAS study in this lesson's readings addresses: Tan and colleagues recorded activity in the nucleus accumbens during feeding and drinking in mice and found that shared ensembles of neurons respond to both, and that manipulating particular neurons alters both behaviours. The lesson from the study is not that one circuit explains eating, which would be a deterministic single-molecule style of claim about a molecule rather than a circuit, but that appetite behaviours with different physiological functions recruit overlapping circuitry, which complicates any account in which hunger and thirst are separate labelled lines. Compare that with the temperature case, where the single-variable loop is comparatively clean, and notice that the difference in tractability is a difference in the biology, not in the quality of the science.
depth.mistake: The common error is to treat a set point as a thermostat with a number in it, so that any failure to return to the original value is evidence that regulation has broken down. Diagnose it with the weight arithmetic: the extrapolation of a fixed daily surplus predicts a linear rise, and real weight trajectories flatten because the surplus itself depends on the new mass and on the changed intake and expenditure, which is the sign that the resting value moves with the conditions rather than being defended at a fixed number. A second error is the inverse, treating the absence of a defended value as evidence that the system is not regulated at all, which ignores the well-characterised feedback signals. The correction is to ask which specific claim is being made: is a target value encoded and defended, is the system settling where flows balance, or is there a mixture? Fever is the clarifying case, because it shows that changing the defended level and failing to regulate look superficially similar in the number but are entirely different mechanisms.
depth.application: Nonblocking task. Write a one-page regulation audit of one variable of your choice from temperature, hydration or appetite. Cover four points. First, name the sensors, the integrating structure and at least two effectors, and label each as established textbook material or as an inference. Second, compute one quantity from the lesson's arithmetic that applies to your variable and show the working, stating which constants you invented. Third, state whether your variable is better described by a set point, a settling point, or a mixture, and name the observation that would change your answer. Fourth, describe the observable behaviour that would be expected if the variable were regulated only by simple negative feedback with no anticipation, and compare it with what actually happens in a familiar situation such as drinking after a salty meal. Self-review rubric: full credit requires the computed quantity with its constants stated, an explicit choice among the three frameworks with the reason, and a described observable rather than an anatomical prediction. No credit for a page that assumes regulation implies a fixed target.
depth.summary: Temperature shows physiological regulation in its clearest form: sensors, a central comparison against a level that fever can raise, and identifiable effectors, with the arithmetic showing why raising the temperature of a whole body costs a substantial fraction of a day's energy. Feeding shares the feedback architecture and is more contested, because the evidence fits an account in which intake and expenditure settle at a value that shifts with conditions, and the textbook's set point framing is disputed in the review cited here. Thirst sits between the two, and modern circuit-level work shows that hunger and thirst recruit overlapping populations, which complicates labelled-line accounts of appetite. Across all three, the transferable skill is to separate a well-evidenced mechanism from an inference about what the system as a whole is controlling.

lessons.title: Circadian biology beyond sleep: an internal clock that times many systems
lessons.explanation: Objective: describe the molecular and circuit basis of the daily clock, distinguish an endogenous rhythm from a response to the environment, explain entrainment and the free-running period, and recognise that the clock reaches far beyond sleep. Begin with the definition that keeps the rest of the lesson honest. A circadian rhythm is an endogenous oscillation with a period of about a day that persists in the absence of external timing cues and that can be reset by them. That definition has two testable clauses, and both matter: the rhythm must continue without cues, which distinguishes it from a simple response to light or to activity, and it must be resettable, which distinguishes it from a fixed internal timer. The circuit is well localised. The suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus is the principal mammalian clock, and the 2023 review by Starnes and Jones, 'Inputs and Outputs of the Mammalian Circadian Clock', is organised exactly the way the anatomy is: section 2 covers the afferent projections that carry light information to the nucleus, section 3 covers hormonal inputs, and section 4 covers the efferent projections through which the clock influences the rest of the body. That structure is the answer to the 'beyond sleep' question, because the outputs listed in section 4 are what make the clock a regulator of physiology rather than a sleep switch. Inside the cells, the clock is a transcription-translation feedback loop in which clock proteins drive the expression of their own repressors, taking about a day per cycle. The 2015 study by Kudo, Block and Colwell in ASN Neuro examines how one clock gene, Period1, links that molecular loop to the electrical activity of the neurons themselves, which is the step that turns a cellular oscillator into a signal other systems can read.
lessons.example: Compute the period arithmetic, because the difference between the internal period and the solar day is exactly what forces the clock to be resettable. The human free-running period measured under controlled conditions is commonly reported at slightly more than 24 hours, with values of the order of 24.1 to 24.2 hours. Take an illustrative value of 24.18 hours. The daily drift is 24.18 minus 24, which is 0.18 hours, or 10.8 minutes per day when multiplied by 60. Over a week the drift is 0.18 multiplied by 7, which is 1.26 hours; over a month of 30 days it is 5.4 hours; over a year it is 0.18 multiplied by 365, which is about 66 hours, or nearly three days. A person whose clock were not reset would therefore be living a day nearly three hours and a quarter longer than the solar day by the end of a week, which is why entrainment is not a detail but a requirement. Now consider a jet lag computation with the same logic. Crossing six time zones requires shifting the clock by six hours. If the clock shifts at about one hour per day when the day is lengthened and about one and a half hours per day when it is shortened, which is the common textbook asymmetry, then travelling west, which lengthens the local day, needs about 6 divided by 1, that is six days, while travelling east, which shortens it, needs about 6 divided by 1.5, that is four days. The constants are illustrative and individual variation is large, but the asymmetry is a real and repeatedly reported pattern, and the arithmetic shows why a shift of several hours cannot be absorbed in a single night.
lessons.question: A person works a rotating shift schedule and reports digestive and metabolic problems as well as sleep trouble. A colleague suggests this is simply because they sleep less. What does the organisation of the circadian system suggest about that explanation, and what evidence would test it?
lessons.answer: The suprachiasmatic nucleus sends outputs to many systems beyond the sleep-wake circuitry, so a disrupted clock can misalign peripheral physiology independently of total sleep time; a test would compare a schedule that shortens sleep while keeping timing regular against a schedule that keeps sleep duration but shifts timing.
lessons.distractor: The suggestion is correct, because the circadian system only controls sleep and any other symptoms must be consequences of sleep loss.
lessons.correction: The clock's outputs are not confined to sleep regulation, as the afferent and efferent projections in the review make clear, and many tissues contain their own oscillators that can be uncoupled from the central clock when behaviour changes abruptly. The two candidate explanations therefore make different predictions: the sleep-duration account predicts that problems track total sleep time while the timing account predicts they track the mismatch between internal and external time, even when sleep duration is held constant. Comparing two schedules that differ in one variable while holding the other fixed is what separates them, and it is the design the question asks for. This is a research question about groups, not a diagnosis for an individual, which would require a clinician.

depth.definitions: A circadian rhythm is an endogenous oscillation of about 24 hours that persists without external cues and can be reset by them. Entrainment is the process by which an external cycle adjusts the period and phase of the internal clock so that it stays aligned with the environment. The free-running period is the period the clock adopts in the absence of cues, known as constant conditions. A zeitgeber is a timing cue, light being the strongest. Phase is the position of the rhythm in time; a phase response curve describes how a cue delivered at a given phase shifts the rhythm, advancing it or delaying it. The transcription-translation feedback loop is the molecular oscillator, in which clock gene products regulate their own transcription. Peripheral clocks are oscillators in tissues outside the suprachiasmatic nucleus. Chronotype is an individual's habitual timing of sleep and activity. Prerequisites: the two-process account of sleep regulation and what it does and does not establish (lesson 45), and the difference between a regulated variable and a fixed target (lesson 58).
depth.mechanism: At the molecular level, a heterodimer of clock proteins activates the transcription of period and cryptochrome genes, whose protein products accumulate, enter the nucleus and inhibit their own activation, after which they are degraded and the cycle restarts. Because the accumulation, inhibition and degradation each take time, the loop's period is close to but not exactly a day, which is why the system needs entrainment. The 2015 study by Kudo, Block and Colwell in this lesson's readings asks how one component of that loop, Period1, relates to the electrical activity of suprachiasmatic neurons, which matters because a molecular oscillator is useless as a signal until it modulates something another system can read. Light reaches the clock through a specialised retinal pathway, and the review's section 2 lays out the afferent projections and the role of the melanopsin-containing cells that report overall light level rather than image detail, which is why the clock responds to brightness and to the blue end of the spectrum rather than to pictures. The limitation to state is that the core loop is well-established in animals, while the mapping from clock state to human disease risk is inferential and heavily influenced by observational studies of shift workers, whose exposures are confounded with occupation, sleep loss and social factors.
depth.secondExample: Take a contrasting case where timing rather than duration is varied deliberately: a controlled protocol that holds sleep opportunity constant while shifting the timing of the day. The relevant published literature includes the misalignment studies summarised in the 2020 review in Military Medical Research by Guo and colleagues, whose section on the entrainment range of circadian rhythms in non-24-hour environments such as submarines is a concrete case. In such environments the imposed day length may differ from the internal period by more than the clock can absorb, and the review discusses how far entrainment can stretch before the rhythm breaks down and free-runs. Compare this with the ordinary daylight case where the day is exactly 24 hours and the free-running period of about 24.18 hours is compressed a little each day. The quantitative contrast between 'a small daily correction' and 'a correction larger than the mechanism can make' is the analytic content: entrainment works within a limited range, and outside that range the system reverts to free-running, which is exactly the state the lesson's period arithmetic describes. This also gives the correct reading of non-24-hour sleep patterns in people without light perception, which are described in that literature as free-running rather than as a pathology of willpower.
depth.mistake: The common error is to treat the clock as a sleep regulator that happens to have side effects, and therefore to treat circadian problems as sleep problems. Diagnose it by asking what happens to a peripheral tissue whose local clock is uncoupled from the central clock by an abrupt change in meal timing or activity while sleep is unchanged; if the clock's outputs were restricted to sleep, no such uncoupling would be possible, since the peripheral oscillator would have nothing to run on. A second error is to treat the endogenous rhythm as evidence that behaviour is unchangeable, which inverts the point: an endogenous rhythm with a period that differs from the day is precisely why the system must be adjustable, and why scheduled light and timing behaviour are potent levers. A third error is to overstate the specificity of any single mechanism, for example attributing all metabolic consequences of shift work to one clock gene or one hormone; the literature is a mixture of strong mechanistic work in animals and observational associations in humans, and the two should be cited separately.
depth.application: Nonblocking task, and it is an observational design exercise rather than advice about your own schedule, which is a matter for a clinician if you have concerns. Design a hypothetical two-week study comparing sleep-duration and circadian-timing accounts of a measured outcome such as self-rated daytime alertness. Write one page covering four points. First, define the two arms of the study, and specify what is held constant in each and what differs, so that the two accounts make different predictions. Second, name the outcome measure and state one way it could be biased by expectancy and how you would reduce that. Third, compute the number of days the shift should take to be absorbed under the one-hour-per-day assumption and under the one-and-a-half-hour-per-day assumption, showing the arithmetic and stating that both rates are illustrative. Fourth, state one limitation of the design that no amount of additional participants would fix. Self-review rubric: full credit requires the two arms to differ in exactly one variable, the arithmetic to be shown with constants labelled as illustrative, and the unfixeable limitation to be about design or construct rather than about cost. No credit for a page that prescribes a schedule for a real person.
depth.summary: The circadian system is an endogenous oscillator with a period slightly longer than 24 hours, built from a transcription-translation feedback loop inside cells and organised centrally by the suprachiasmatic nucleus, which receives light information on a specialised pathway and sends outputs to many bodily systems. The small daily mismatch between internal period and solar day is why entrainment exists, and the arithmetic shows both the size of the daily correction and the impossibility of large shifts in one night. The clock's reach beyond sleep is the point: peripheral tissues have their own oscillators and can be uncoupled from the central clock, which is why timing and duration are separate variables that a good study must manipulate independently.
