lessons.title: Capstone: is the brain a computer, and where does the metaphor break?
lessons.explanation: Objective: state what the computational metaphor of the brain asserts, give a concrete demonstration of where it illuminates and where it misleads, and evaluate claims that use it in either direction. Begin by making the metaphor precise, because it is used loosely. In its useful form it asserts four things: neural activity carries information, transformations of that information can be described as operations, the operations can be implemented in more than one physical substrate, and a description at the level of operations can be explanatory even when the implementation details are unknown. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry on the computational theory of mind is the cleanest free account of how this claim has been formulated, and its structure is a good test of whether a claim is really computational: section 1 sets out Turing machines, section 3 the classical computational theory of mind with machine functionalism and the representational theory of mind, section 4 neural networks with the subsections on the relation between networks and classical computation and on computational neuroscience, and section 5 the unresolved questions about computation and representation, including whether a computation must be formal. Read section 5 especially, because that is where the entry itself identifies the live disagreements rather than the settled parts. The metaphor's most serious failure mode is not that it is false, which is too coarse a verdict, but that it invites a specific method and then rewards its results prematurely. That is the argument of the 2017 paper by Jonas and Kording, 'Could a Neuroscientist Understand a Microprocessor?', which takes a real processor and applies the tools of modern neuroscience to it.
lessons.example: Work through what the Jonas and Kording study did, because the demonstration is the argument. The authors took a chip that they could describe exhaustively and applied the standard methods of the field to it. The paper's section headings show the list: connectomics, in which the transistor connections were reconstructed, lesioning single transistors one at a time, and other analyses in the same family. The result they report is that these analyses produced results that looked like neuroscience findings and did not reveal the processor's function. This is a controlled demonstration: the ground truth was known, the methods were the field's own, and the conclusions those methods supported were wrong or uninformative. Now the arithmetic of the analogy. The processor model they used, the MOS 6502, contains a few thousand transistors, so its component count is on the order of ten to the third or fourth. A human brain contains on the order of eighty to a hundred billion neurons, roughly ten to the eleventh, and each neuron may receive thousands of synapses, so a crude count of synaptic connections is of the order of ten to the fourteenth or fifteenth. Compute the ratio of the connection counts: ten to the fourteenth divided by ten to the fourth is ten to the tenth, that is ten billion times more connections. The point of the comparison is not that a bigger number makes the task impossible but that the two systems differ by so many orders of magnitude that an argument from 'we understand computers, therefore the method transfers' has no basis: the analogy is between a system whose every element can be enumerated and one whose elements cannot currently be enumerated at all. The constants here are order-of-magnitude textbook values and should be labelled as such.
lessons.question: A researcher argues that because the brain performs computations, a complete account of the brain must be given in the vocabulary of computer science, and that psychological descriptions will eventually be replaced. Using the processor study and the philosophy entry, state what is overstated in that claim and what part of it is defensible.
lessons.answer: Defensible: that information-processing descriptions at a level above the physical implementation can be explanatory and that some transformations are usefully described as operations, with the support that the same function can be implemented in different substrates. Overstated: the inference from that fact to the replacement of other descriptions, and the assumption that the vocabulary of computer science is uniquely privileged, since the entry's section 5 records the unresolved disputes about what counts as a computation and about representation, and the processor study shows that a computable system can fail to yield its function under an information-processing analysis applied without knowing the right level.
lessons.distractor: Defensible: nothing, because the processor study shows that computational descriptions of the brain are worthless. Overstated: nothing, because the brain is a physical system and all physical systems perform computations.
lessons.correction: Both halves of that answer are wrong in symmetrical ways. The processor study does not show that computational descriptions are worthless; it shows that a particular set of methods, mainly structural reconstruction and single-element lesions, fails to recover function even in a system whose function is known, which is evidence about the sufficiency of those methods rather than about the metaphor. And the claim that all physical systems perform computations is a definitional move rather than a finding, since without criteria for which physical processes count as implementing which computations, the statement is true of everything and therefore explains nothing. The careful answer keeps three things apart: the claim that information is carried and transformed, which is well-supported; the claim that a particular formal vocabulary is the right one, which is contested; and the claim that other levels of description will be replaced, which does not follow from either.

depth.definitions: Computation, in the sense relevant here, is the transformation of representations according to rules. A formal or syntactic account holds that what makes something a computation is the manipulation of symbols by their form rather than their content. Implementation means the physical realisation of an operation; multiple realizability is the claim that one operation can be realised in different substrates. A level of description is a vocabulary and set of entities in which explanations are given, for example the physical, the circuit, the information-processing and the behavioural. Reverse inference is the inference from a measured signal to a mental state, treated earlier in this course. A metaphor here means a transfer of vocabulary from one domain to another that carries methodological commitments with it. Prerequisites: reverse inference and its selectivity requirement (lesson 29), the necessity and sufficiency distinction (lesson 28), and the evidence hierarchy for causal claims (lesson 50).
depth.mechanism: The metaphor's illumination comes from a specific methodological success: treating a neural response as carrying information about a stimulus, and asking how much and of what kind, has generated measurable predictions, and treating a circuit as implementing a transformation has yielded testable models such as those for population coding earlier in this unit. Its failure modes are equally specific and can be enumerated. First, structural completeness does not imply functional understanding, which is what the processor study demonstrates directly. Second, the metaphor tends to license the assumption that the system has a clean division of labour, so that a structure's function can be read off its activity, which is the reverse inference problem; the processor has registers with defined roles, and brains are less obligingly partitioned. Third, the metaphor suggests that information is transmitted and stored in defined units, whereas the evidence supports distributed, context-dependent and continuously modulated representations, as the lesson on touch coding illustrates. Fourth, the metaphor is silent about the things brains do that computers are not usually built to do, including maintaining themselves, developing, and being affected by their own history; the philosophy entry's section 4.4 on computational neuroscience shows that the relationship between network models and neuroscience is itself an unsettled question, which is the honest place to leave it rather than declaring a winner.
depth.secondExample: Take a contrasting case where a computational description has been genuinely productive, so that the lesson does not become a general attack on the metaphor: the basal-ganglia account of action selection, in which competing actions are represented by populations whose activity suppresses one another and a selected action emerges when one population escapes inhibition. That is a computational description at the level of operations, it generates predictions that have been tested by manipulating the relevant populations, and it does not require anyone to assert that the brain is a computer in a metaphysical sense. Compare it with the processor study, which found that structural methods did not recover function. The two together give the balanced conclusion: the productive use of computational vocabulary arises when the model makes a specific prediction about what happens under a manipulation, and the misleading use arises when a structural or correlational finding is dressed up in computational language without such a prediction. Ask of any claim that the brain computes X: what would be different if it did not, and what measurement would show it.
depth.mistake: The most common error is to argue about the metaphor as though it were either true or false in general, and then to pick a side based on an example that suits it. Diagnose it by asking what observation would count against each side, and note how rarely such an answer is forthcoming: conclusive evidence against the general claim is difficult to specify, which is a sign that the dispute is being conducted at the wrong level of precision. The correction is to translate the general question into specific ones, such as whether a particular representation is carried by a rate code or a timing code, as in the auditory lesson, or whether a structure's activity is necessary or merely correlated, as in the causal-inference lesson. A second error is the reverse of the first, dismissing the metaphor entirely because it has been overused, which throws away the measured successes in information-theoretic analysis and in model-based accounts of action selection. The disciplined position is to ask which specific claim is being made and what would falsify it.
depth.application: Nonblocking capstone task, worth treating as the level's main written exercise. Choose one headline claim of the form the brain computes X, whether from a news item or from a paper you have read. Write two pages. First, restate the claim at three levels: the physical or anatomical finding, the information-processing claim, and the behavioural claim, and mark which of the three the original evidence actually supports. Second, state what a computational version of the claim predicts that a structural version does not, and give the measurement that would distinguish them. Third, name the comparison set or manipulation that would address the reverse inference problem for this claim. Fourth, write the strongest honest sentence you can in support of the claim and the strongest honest sentence against it, each with the evidence you would want. Self-review rubric: full credit requires all three levels to be distinguished, a prediction that is genuinely computational rather than anatomical, an explicit comparison set or manipulation, and both directions stated with their evidence rather than with rhetoric. Partial credit for a clear restatement at three levels without a discriminating prediction. No credit for a verdict, in either direction, that does not state what would have changed your mind.
depth.summary: The computational metaphor of the brain asserts that neural activity carries information, that transformations of it can be described as operations, that descriptions at that level can be explanatory, and that the same operation can be realised differently. Its productive uses involve predictions that a purely structural account would not make, as in information-theoretic analyses and model-based accounts of action selection. Its failure modes are equally concrete: structural completeness does not deliver functional understanding, as the processor study shows; the metaphor encourages reading a structure's function off its activity, which is reverse inference; and it under-describes representation, self-maintenance and history. The capstone skill is not to decide whether the metaphor is true but to convert any general claim into one that names its level, its prediction, and its falsifier.

readings.title: Could a Neuroscientist Understand a Microprocessor? (Jonas and Kording, PLoS Computational Biology, 2017)
readings.note: Read the Abstract and Author Summary, then the sections 'An engineered model organism', 'What does it mean to understand a system' and 'What would a satisfying understanding of the processor look like?', and then the Results subsections on connectomics and on lesioning a single transistor at a time. The Results list is the argument, so read the headings as a sequence of attempted methods and note what each one recovered. Open access. This is the central reading for the capstone.

readings.title: The Computational Theory of Mind (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
readings.note: Read section 1 on Turing machines, section 3 on the classical computational theory of mind including 3.1 machine functionalism and 3.2 the representational theory of mind, section 4 on neural networks with 4.1 on the relation between networks and classical computation and 4.4 on computational neuroscience, and then section 5, especially 5.1 'Computation as formal' and 5.2 on externalism about mental content. Section 5 is where the entry identifies live disagreements, so it is the part to read slowly. Openly available, and revised periodically, so check the entry's own revision date rather than assuming a fixed edition.

visual.title: Three levels, one metaphor: where it illuminates and where it breaks
visual.description: A labelled schema separating physical, information-processing and behavioural levels, then showing the processor demonstration and the criteria for a productive computational claim.
steps: Panel 1: three stacked boxes labelled from bottom to top: 'physical and anatomical level: cells, connections, signals', 'information-processing level: representations and operations', 'behavioural level: what the system does'. Arrows drawn both up and down between them, with a note that a finding at one level does not by itself license a claim at another.

Panel 2: a chip drawn with a labelled transistor grid and an arrow to a list of attempted methods labelled 'connectomics', 'lesion one transistor at a time', with a result box stating 'function not recovered despite ground truth being known'.

Panel 3: a scale comparison drawn to logarithmic order of magnitude: 'processor: about 10 to the 4 components' beside 'brain: about 10 to the 11 neurons, 10 to the 14 or 15 synapses', with the ratio written as about 10 to the 10.

Panel 4: a successful computational claim drawn as a loop: a model of competing action populations, an arrow to a prediction about what happens under manipulation, an arrow to a measurement, and an arrow back to the model labelled 'the claim earns its vocabulary by predicting'.

Panel 5: a symmetric pair of failure boxes. Left: 'an anatomical finding dressed in computational language with no manipulation or comparison set'. Right: 'the metaphor dismissed wholesale, discarding the measured successes'. Both marked with a cross.

Panel 6: a checklist boxed beside the panels with four items: which level is being claimed; what the computational version predicts that the structural version does not; what comparison set or manipulation addresses reverse inference; and what would falsify the claim.

questions.prompt: A robotic arm is built with a purely feedback controller whose sensory loop takes about 33 milliseconds and whose targets move unpredictably, and it achieves smooth slow movements but fails at fast reaches. Which change follows from the lesson's control-theory reasoning?
questions.answer: Add a feedforward element that issues the initial command from a prediction of the movement's consequences, so corrections are applied to a predicted rather than a fully realised state.
questions.distractor: Reduce the loop time to zero, since any remaining delay is the sole cause of the failure.
questions.correction: Eliminating delay is not available: the physical round trip through actuators and sensors is the constraint, and the lesson's arithmetic shows that most of the delay in a human voluntary reaction is central rather than peripheral, so shortening conduction alone would not close the gap. Feedforward control is the indicated change because a fast reach of a few hundred milliseconds allows only a few corrections, so most of the trajectory must be computed in advance and corrected against a prediction. The reasoning also explains why the system does well at slow targets: where feedback is affordable, the simple loop is adequate, which is the comparative evidence the argument rests on.

questions.prompt: A study reports that participants who count more heartbeats accurately also score higher on a self-report measure of body awareness, and concludes that interoception drives body awareness. Which feature of the method most limits that conclusion?
questions.answer: The task can be completed using a belief about one's heart rate rather than an internal signal, so the association may reflect self-knowledge or reporting style rather than sensitivity.
questions.distractor: The sample was too small, because correlations based on small samples are always uninterpretable regardless of the measure used.
questions.correction: Sample size affects precision and not the direction of a confound, so it is not the limiting feature here. The critical issue is that the accuracy score mixes a signal with the participant's belief about their own heart rate, which is why a count near an assumed rate can be produced without sensing anything, and which is also why different scoring rules yield different numbers from the same data. The correction is to use a task in which the internal signal is independently measured, and to treat the measure's components separately rather than as one index of a trait.

questions.prompt: A food-policy model assumes that a fixed daily energy surplus of 500 kilocalories produces steady weight gain for several years, and is surprised that observed weight plateaus. Using the regulation frameworks in the lesson, diagnose the model's error.
questions.answer: It treats a settled system as an open one: as mass changes, the energy cost of maintenance and movement and the resulting intake both change, so the surplus is not constant and a resting value that shifts with conditions is expected.
questions.distractor: The surplus has been miscalculated and should be about 3500 kilocalories per day, since that is the constant that converts energy to mass.
questions.correction: The 3500 kilocalories per pound figure is a conversion rule, not a daily surplus, and the model's arithmetic of 500 divided by 3500 giving about 0.143 pounds per day is correct within its own assumption. The error is the assumption of a fixed surplus over years rather than the conversion constant. As mass rises, energy expenditure rises with it and intake is influenced by many signals, so weight approaches a value where flows balance, which is the settling-point account rather than a defended fixed target. Fever is the useful contrast: there the regulated level itself changes, which shows that changing a level and failing to regulate can look similar in a single number while being different mechanisms.

questions.prompt: A researcher proposes to study jet lag by confining participants to a room with a 25-hour day, reasoning that this will simply delay sleep by an hour each night. Using the free-running period and entrainment-range concepts, assess the proposal.
questions.answer: The imposed day is longer than the internal period of about 24.2 hours, so the daily correction is within the range a normally entrainable clock can absorb, but as the imposed period grows further the correction can exceed the range and the rhythm will free-run rather than continue to entrain.
questions.distractor: The proposal cannot work at all, because circadian rhythms are fixed internal periods that cannot be adjusted in any environment.
questions.correction: The internal period is close to but not equal to a day, which is precisely why the rhythm must be adjustable and why scheduling light can shift it; a fixed, unadjustable clock would be a different claim and would contradict the evidence that light resets the system. The substantive point is quantitative: the size of the required daily correction must be compared with the range the clock can absorb. With an internal period of about 24.18 hours, a 25-hour day asks for a correction of about 0.82 hours, and the review in the readings shows that this kind of imposed day can be tolerated up to a limit, beyond which the system drifts into free-running rather than holding the imposed phase.

questions.prompt: A press release states that a new study reveals how the brain computes the value of a reward, and the study itself reports that a set of neurons responds more strongly to unexpected than to expected rewards. Which sentence best characterises what the evidence supports?
questions.answer: The evidence supports an information-processing description at the level of a response that tracks a discrepancy between expectation and outcome, and the word computes adds a claim about operations and implementation that a response difference has not established.
questions.distractor: The evidence supports the computational claim completely, because a response that tracks a discrepancy is by definition the implementation of a computation.
questions.correction: Tracking a discrepancy is a property of the response, and describing it as computing assumes a level of analysis and an implementation that were not measured. The processor demonstration in the readings is the relevant caution, because it shows that a system whose operations are fully known can still fail to yield its function under structural and single-element analyses, so a response difference cannot carry the whole of a computational claim. What would strengthen the claim is a prediction that the computational version makes and the structural version does not, together with a comparison set or manipulation that addresses whether the response is selective for this variable.

questions.prompt: A functional imaging study reports that activity in V1 varies with the orientation of a grating, and a commentary concludes that V1 is where edges are computed. Separately, a single-unit study reports that V1 cells have oriented receptive fields, and the same commentary treats the two findings as converging. Explain what is established, what is missing from the convergence argument, and why pooling and receptive-field evidence are not the same as implementation evidence.
questions.answer: What is established is that V1 activity carries orientation information and that single units are orientation-selective; what is missing is any demonstration of the operation by which the orientation signal is produced or used, since a population response can carry a variable without the region being the site where the operation is implemented.
questions.distractor: Both findings establish the computation because a response that covaries with orientation and a receptive field tuned to orientation are two independent measurements of the same operation.
questions.correction: Two measurements of a correlated variable are not two measurements of an operation. A BOLD contrast measures a haemodynamic correlate of local activity and a receptive field measures what changes a cell's firing, so both are descriptions of what varies with the stimulus rather than of how the transformation is performed. The lesson's convergence arithmetic shows a plausible feedforward mechanism, and the same arithmetic shows that pooling alone produces larger and more specialised fields, so a receptive-field hierarchy is compatible with several implementations including recurrent amplification. What would close the gap is an intervention that changes the hypothesised operation and produces the predicted change in the response, together with a check that the effect is selective rather than a general change in responsiveness.

questions.prompt: A listener hears a complex tone whose energy lies at 200, 400 and 600 hertz and reports a pitch corresponding to 200 hertz, even though a control stimulus with energy only at 200 hertz is judged to have a slightly different quality. Design a comparison that would distinguish a place account from a timing account of the reported pitch, and state what each account predicts.
questions.answer: Compare pitch judgements for complex tones whose fundamental is below the range where phase locking is reliable with tones whose fundamental is inside that range, and add tones in which the lower harmonics are masked or removed; a timing account predicts pitch is preserved while the periodicity is available regardless of where the energy lies on the basilar membrane, whereas a place account predicts the judgement follows the position of maximal excitation.
questions.distractor: Compare loudness judgements for the same complex tones, since a place account and a timing account make opposite predictions about the total energy reaching the cochlea.
questions.correction: Loudness is a different perceptual dimension from pitch and both accounts can be made to predict the same total energy, so the comparison would not discriminate between them. The discriminating design has to vary the thing the accounts disagree about, which is whether the percept follows the position of maximal basilar membrane excitation or the periodicity extracted across the population. Because the reported pitch in the example corresponds to a component with little or no energy, a pure place code for that component cannot account for the judgement, which is why the timing account is invoked; a proper test manipulates the availability of periodicity and the position of excitation separately and asks which one the judgement tracks.

questions.prompt: A study finds that the cortical territory devoted to the fingertip is much larger per square centimetre of skin than the territory devoted to the forearm, and concludes that the fingertip representation has higher spatial resolution. A second study finds that fingertip two-point discrimination thresholds are much finer than forearm thresholds. Explain how the two findings relate, and identify the step in the reasoning that is not licensed by either measurement alone.
questions.answer: The territory difference is a magnification claim about how much cortex is allocated per unit of skin, and the threshold difference is a behavioural resolution claim; both are consistent with denser innervation and smaller receptive fields at the fingertip, but neither alone establishes that the cortical territory is what produces the finer resolution, since receptor density and peripheral convergence could account for the thresholds without any cortical contribution.
questions.distractor: The findings establish the same claim from two directions, because more cortical territory necessarily produces finer discrimination at the corresponding skin site.
questions.correction: Territory and threshold are different quantities measured in different units, so agreement between them is consistency rather than proof of a mechanism. The unlicensed step is the attribution of the behavioural threshold to the cortical allocation, because the peripheral factors of receptor density, receptive field size and convergence ratio were computed in the lesson and can produce the threshold difference on their own. To license the cortical claim you would need a manipulation or comparison in which peripheral innervation is held constant while cortical territory is varied, or a case in which the two dissociate, which is exactly the kind of test the map lessons require before a magnification finding is read as a resolution mechanism.

questions.prompt: In a controlled experiment, a local anaesthetic block of a peripheral nerve in a person with chronic limb pain reduces reported pain substantially but not completely. One investigator says this proves the pain was nociceptive; another says it proves nothing about mechanism. Using the necessity and sufficiency distinction, adjudicate.
questions.answer: The block is evidence that input through that nerve contributed to the pain, which is a partial necessity finding for that pathway, and it does not establish the mechanistic descriptor, because the residual pain shows that other contributions are present and because a modulation framework predicts exactly this partial reduction.
questions.distractor: The block proves the pain was nociceptive, since blocking nociceptive fibres reduced the pain and any remaining report must be measurement error.
questions.correction: A reduction produced by blocking a pathway is evidence about the contribution of that pathway, and the size of the remaining report is evidence about everything else, so treating the residual as error discards the most informative part of the result. Mechanism classification requires more than one intervention, because the same partial reduction is predicted by accounts in which peripheral input and central modulation both contribute; the lesson on pain modulation makes this explicit, and the dispute over mechanistic descriptors for chronic pain shows that researchers using similar evidence disagree about classification. The careful statement is that the block established a contribution from the blocked fibres, and that any claim about the descriptor needs additional evidence about the other contributing processes.

questions.prompt: An engineer builds a balance aid that reports body tilt by averaging signals from a fluid sensor whose output decays over several seconds and from a camera that measures the visual horizon. During a long constant-velocity turn the aid reports a tilt that is not present. Explain the cause in terms of the signals available, and state why a purely reflexive correction loop cannot fix the problem on its own.
questions.answer: The fluid sensor reports angular acceleration rather than position and its output decays with a time constant, so during prolonged motion it supplies a misleading residual signal that the average treats as evidence; a reflexive loop using that signal would generate a correction that is wrong for the same reason, so the aid needs a gravity-referenced or independent position cue to resolve the ambiguity.
questions.distractor: The averaging step is at fault because averaging two signals always produces an intermediate value, and the correct remedy is to use the camera alone at all times.
questions.correction: Averaging is a reasonable way to combine partial evidence and the failure is not in the combination as such but in the fact that one input has a decaying acceleration signal masquerading as position while the other has an ambiguity of its own, since a visual scene can be ambiguous about which way is up. The biological system faces the identical problem, which is why the vestibular organs are paired with gravity-sensing otoliths and with other cues, and why the tilt-versus-linear-acceleration ambiguity is described as inherent to the otolith signal alone. A reflexive loop is insufficient because a reflex acts on the error it is given, and the error is itself corrupted; resolving the ambiguity requires an independent signal or an internal model, not a faster reflex.

questions.prompt: A commentary states that an experiment recorded a scalp potential beginning several hundred milliseconds before a voluntary movement and a reported awareness of intention about 200 milliseconds before the movement, and concludes that the brain decides before the person is aware. Reconstruct the argument as the commentary states it, then identify the two inferential steps that the source material does not licence.
questions.answer: The commentary infers that the onset of an averaged scalp potential marks the moment of a specific decision in each trial, and that the participant's report of awareness is an accurate timing measure; the first step ignores that averaging stochastic activity accumulating to a threshold produces a similar ramp without a discrete decision event, and the second ignores that the report derives from a subjectively judged clock position over intervals of a few hundred milliseconds.
questions.distractor: The commentary's argument is sound because the scalp potential and the reported awareness time were measured independently of one another, which rules out any shared measurement error.
questions.correction: Independent measurement of the two quantities does not make either one valid for the purpose, and shared error is not the only threat to inference. The accumulator account in the readings shows concretely that a ramp in the average can arise from ongoing noisy activity crossing a threshold, so the onset of the average does not locate a decision within individual trials, which is the first unlicensed step. The second is that the awareness time is itself an estimate produced by the participant, with the sources of error and bias that any such judgement carries. Both points concern the inference from measurement to mechanism, which is why the empirical dispute is about what the waveform can bear rather than about whether the recordings were made.

questions.prompt: A magazine article states that inflammation in the body causes low mood, citing a study in which people with higher circulating inflammatory markers reported more symptoms of low mood. Explain what the design supports, and correct the single-molecule framing using the idea of coordinated sickness behaviour and dose- and timing-dependence.
questions.answer: The design supports an association between a marker of inflammation and reported mood symptoms in the sample studied, and it does not establish that inflammation causes the mood change; the single-molecule framing is also wrong because immune signals act through several routes and produce coordinated changes whose expression depends on dose, timing and context rather than on one substance producing one feeling.
questions.distractor: The design establishes causation because the inflammatory markers were measured objectively with an assay rather than being self-reported.
questions.correction: Objectively measured predictors do not establish direction or rule out confounding, and observational designs of this kind cannot distinguish inflammation causing mood change from mood change and its associated behaviour affecting inflammation, nor from a third factor such as sleep disruption or illness affecting both. The mechanistic correction is separate: the routes from immune signals to the brain include neural and circumventricular pathways as well as local signalling at the barrier, so the relevant description is a coordinated set of behavioural and physiological changes rather than a single molecule with a single effect. The lesson's application task is exactly this exercise of checking whether an internal or immune signal was independently measured and what the design leaves open.

questions.prompt: Two frameworks are applied to the same data on body temperature and body weight. For temperature, a raised regulated level during fever explains why a person feels cold while their temperature climbs; for weight, a settling-point account explains why mass changes when the environment changes and then rests at a new value. A student concludes that because both frameworks use feedback, they are the same claim. Diagnose the error and state what distinguishes them observationally.
questions.answer: Both frameworks do use feedback, so similarity of mechanism is not the difference; what distinguishes them is whether a specific target value is encoded and defended, which predicts a return to the original value after the condition that produced the deviation is removed, whereas a settling account predicts rest at a new value determined by the balance of inflows and outflows.
questions.distractor: They are the same claim, because any system with negative feedback necessarily has a target value at which the feedback error is zero.
questions.correction: Negative feedback requires an error signal, and the error signal requires a reference, but the reference need not be a fixed encoded target: it can be the level at which flows balance, which is the core of the settling account and the argument the review in the readings makes about human body weight. Fever is the clarifying case for the opposite reason, because it shows a genuinely adjusted reference, and it is why the two situations can look alike in a single number while differing in mechanism. Observationally, the discriminating test is removal or reversal of the condition and observation of whether the system returns to the original value or rests at a new one.

questions.prompt: A study of rotating shift workers reports both reduced total sleep and disrupted circadian timing, and finds that metabolic measures are worse in the group with greater timing disruption even after statistically controlling for sleep duration. A reader objects that controlling for duration is meaningless because the two variables are correlated. Assess the objection and state what would strengthen the timing account.
questions.answer: The objection is partly right that a statistical control in a correlated observational design cannot cleanly separate the two variables, and the timing account would be strengthened by a design that manipulates timing while holding sleep opportunity constant, or by a measure of internal phase such as a marker rhythm collected alongside sleep duration.
questions.distractor: The objection is wrong because statistical control is the definitive method for separating correlated variables, so the study already establishes that timing rather than duration is responsible.
questions.correction: Statistical control adjusts for the variable as measured and cannot remove confounding from variables that are not measured at all or that are measured with error, and it certainly cannot establish direction, so neither the objection nor the claim is fully right. What would strengthen the timing account is an experimental or quasi-experimental design in which timing is shifted while sleep opportunity is held constant, together with a phase marker that is not derived from the behaviour being studied, which is the logic the lesson's application task asks you to construct. Note also that the clock sends outputs to many systems beyond sleep, so the mechanism for a timing effect independent of sleep duration is available rather than merely conceivable.

questions.prompt: A grant application states that the proposed work will show how the brain computes a specific decision, and describes a plan to record activity from many neurons during the decision task and to fit a model to the recorded activity. Using the criteria for a computational claim and the processor demonstration, state what the plan can and cannot deliver, and rewrite the aim so that it is falsifiable.
questions.answer: Recording and fitting can deliver a description of how well the recorded activity predicts the decision and which variables the activity tracks, and it cannot deliver an implementation account of the operation, because a fitted model that reproduces the data is compatible with several generating mechanisms and the processor demonstration shows that a system can be structurally characterised without its function being recovered; a falsifiable aim names the prediction the computational account makes that a non-computational account does not and the manipulation that would test it.
questions.distractor: The plan delivers the computational account because a model fitted to neural activity is by definition the operation that the brain performs.
questions.correction: A fitted model is one candidate mechanism among the set that could produce the observations, and descriptive adequacy is a lower bar than implementation. The processor study makes this concrete: structural and single-element analyses of a fully known system failed to recover its function, so reproducing measurements is not the same as explaining the operation. The rewrite the question asks for is the operational test of whether a claim is computational at all, because if the account predicts nothing that a simpler structural or correlational account does not predict, then the computational vocabulary is decorative rather than load-bearing, and the falsifier has to be stated before the data are collected.

questions.prompt: A clinical service wants to use a questionnaire score to decide which patients need further assessment for a condition characterised by unusual internal sensations. A statistician points out that the questionnaire measures a belief about the body rather than sensitivity, and that the underlying construct has been argued to comprise distinct components. Explain what this implies for the intended use, and why the distinction matters more for individual decisions than for group averages.
questions.answer: If the instrument indexes a belief rather than sensitivity, then a high score identifies people who report unusual internal sensations rather than people with a particular underlying mechanism, so using it to route individuals presumes a correspondence between construct and measure that the instrument does not establish; for group averages a shared mismatch would tend to cancel less visibly than for individual decisions, where a single misclassification has a direct consequence.
questions.distractor: The distinction does not matter for either use, because a questionnaire that correlates with the construct is a valid instrument for individual decisions as well as for group comparisons.
questions.correction: Correlation with a construct in a sample is the minimum requirement and not a licence for individual prediction, because group-level associations can coexist with substantial overlap between individuals and with a measure that is partly driven by a different variable such as reporting tendency or health anxiety. The lesson's arithmetic on the heartbeat-counting score makes the mechanism visible, since the same data produce different numbers under different scoring rules and a belief about heart rate can supply the count without any sensing. The practical consequence is that the instrument can be defensible for research comparisons while remaining unsuited to individual routing, and that adding a task in which the internal signal is independently measured is what would change the picture.

questions.prompt: Design a study that could distinguish three competing accounts of a bodily sensation reported by healthy participants: a peripheral-input account, a predictive or modulatory account, and a timing account in which the sensation depends on when an internal clock signal is sampled. State for each account one prediction that at least one of the others does not make, and name the single measurement that would be most informative if only one could be taken.
questions.answer: The peripheral account predicts that the sensation scales with the independently measured stimulus or afferent signal; the predictive account predicts that manipulating expectation or context changes the sensation while the measured stimulus is held constant; the timing account predicts that the sensation varies with the phase at which the stimulus is delivered relative to a separately measured internal rhythm; the most informative single measurement is an independent record of the peripheral or physiological signal delivered, because without it none of the three accounts can be compared with the input that is being explained.
questions.distractor: The peripheral account predicts that the sensation scales with the measured stimulus, while the other two accounts make no testable predictions and are therefore not scientific alternatives.
questions.correction: All three accounts make testable predictions, and their testability is precisely what makes the design possible: the predictive and timing accounts are discriminated by manipulating expectation and by measuring phase independently of the report, and both require the peripheral measurement to be meaningful because otherwise a change in the percept cannot be attributed to modulation or timing rather than to a change in input. The design also needs the participant's report to be collected in a way that does not presuppose the construct, which is the measurement warning from the interoception lesson. Naming the independently measured input first is the right ordering, because it is the quantity against which all three accounts are evaluated.
